title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether a minimal guarded pipeline — single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration — reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes (300 pairs) using 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, eliminating statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc sensitivity bound based on the archived contingency, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. The run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived and enumerated in the execution manifest described in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is a central NetOps task. Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize device commands but probabilistic generation risks misordering, omission, or unsafe changes. A common mitigation pattern is generate→verify→repair where a deterministic validator (or simulator) serves as a floor‑safety net. Despite many architectural proposals and demonstrations, there are few preregistered paired A/B experiments that quantify how a bounded guarded pipeline changes first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics. Our research question: Can a minimal guarded pipeline (single shared LLM candidate, frozen deterministic validator, ≤1 automated repair iteration) reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation in a paired confirmatory design?
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and system demonstrations show LLMs can translate intent to configuration templates but also document failure modes (hallucination, misordering, overconfidence) that threaten operational safety. Cross‑domain studies (medical QA, code generation) show verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented designs reduce factual errors; NetOps proposals recommend deterministic validators or simulators as floor safety nets. However, few works present preregistered, paired experiments with deterministically generated task banks, frozen validators, and bounded repair budgets. This study situates itself at that intersection and uses a fully archived execution/analysis pipeline to produce reproducible paired counts and intervals (see cited works for closest prior demonstrations and architecture proposals).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered the complete design (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) and froze sampling, analysis, and retry policies before execution. Confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly used a planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40 for power calculations; that numeric assumption is reported here because it materially conditions the preregistered power target.

Design and sampling semantics: The experiment used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds from the frozen task generator. For each seed a single shared LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics) was produced and reused for both arms: baseline (single‑shot acceptance of candidate) and guarded (same candidate validated and subjected to up to one automated repair call if invalid). The preregistered choice to share the initial candidate increases within‑pair correlation and thereby reduces the number of informative discordant pairs relative to independent draws; this choice was fixed in the preregistration because it isolates validator/repair effects on the same generator output.

Model, validator, and scoring: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, canonicalizes outputs to normalized ASTs, and emits binary pass/fail scoring together with violation codes that drive the repair adapter. A successful episode requires the validator to deem required command sequences and dependency constraints satisfied (full intent‑constraint validation). Missingness and retries: the preregistered missingness plan permitted one retry for provider failures; primary analysis treatment drops pairs only if both calls failed ('complete_pair_primary').

Primary estimand and analysis plan: The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes. We also preregistered a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, fixed seed) for the absolute paired difference and exact binomial intervals for repair success. Secondary exploratory checks included sensitivity treatments for missingness and contamination; all analysis code and per‑task artifacts were archived by the run executor and are enumerated in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301 (shared initial generation calls = 300; repair stage model calls invoked = 1). No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy.

Primary outcomes (artifact‑derived): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts derived from the archived analysis were n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). These exact counts were produced by the preregistered deterministic scorer and appear in the archived condition summary used for inference.

Statistical inference (preregistered procedures applied): Exact McNemar two‑sided test on the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. Observed absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729), as recorded in the archived analysis outputs. Repair outcome (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the only initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); exact Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0].

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to the archived contingency: with only one discordant pair (n10 + n01 = 1) the minimum resolvable absolute paired difference equals 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the observed point estimate). Under the paired McNemar framework the test statistic depends solely on discordant counts; a single discordance provides insufficient evidence to reject the null of no paired difference, producing the observed p = 1.00. The bootstrap CI upper bound (0.01) delimits plausible absolute improvement under the run's sampling semantics; it also shows the preregistered target (≈+0.30 absolute gain corresponding to a 50% relative reduction from assumed baseline) is orders of magnitude larger than any effect resolvable by this dataset given the observed near‑ceiling baseline.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The guarded pipeline succeeded in correcting the sole validator‑detected violation, demonstrating that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can remediate some LLM‑generated violations. However, because the empirical baseline pass rate (299/300) contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40), the experiment lacked statistical headroom to evaluate the preregistered large relative effect (≥50% reduction). The inference limit is an artifact of both the unexpectedly high baseline and the shared_initial_candidate pairing semantics that reduce discordant pairs.

Operational implications and design lessons: (1) Difficulty calibration is essential for confirmatory NetOps experiments: designers should preregister and validate that the task bank yields a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence prior to committing full sample size. Possible approaches include adversarial augmentation, curated higher‑difficulty seeds, or explicit target counts of initial failures rather than sole sample‑size targets. (2) Pairing semantics and repair budgets meaningfully affect inferential power and operational realism: sharing the initial generator output reduces cross‑arm variance but lowers informative discordance; independent draws increase discordance potential but change the estimand. (3) When operational claims require runtime guarantees, static deterministic validators should be complemented by emulation or simulation that exercises control‑plane or packet‑level consequences rather than relying on static AST checks alone.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: fixed shared_initial_candidate design increases within‑pair correlation (preregistered). Construct validity: the deterministic validator evaluates canonicalized configurations and constraints but does not execute configurations in a live network; runtime effects are unmeasured. External validity: the synthetic task bank, limited vendor‑template space, single model family (gpt-5-mini), and single validator implementation restrict generality. Conclusion validity: the paucity of discordant pairs (one total) limits statistical power to detect preregistered large effects.

Recommendations for future confirmatory runs: (a) preregister target initial‑failure counts and calibrate the task bank to achieve them before committing the main run; (b) explicitly choose pairing semantics (shared vs independent draws) according to the intended estimand and report their expected impact on discordant counts used in McNemar‑style inference; (c) expand repair budgets or include human‑in‑the‑loop steps when operational claims require higher recovery rates; (d) incorporate emulation/simulation when runtime or reachability consequences are central to the claim.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (300 pairs) evaluating a frozen deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration applied to gpt‑5‑mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid configurations. The single automated repair corrected the only initially invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target because the observed baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should calibrate task difficulty to produce informative initial failures, explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets, and measure runtime semantic effects when operational claims require them. All raw outputs, scorer/validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived by the run executor; consult the execution manifest described in the Disclosure Statement for the complete artifact inventory and deterministic provenance.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
